31105-the-elements-of-agriculture-a-book:
G. E. Waring Jr.'s Elements of Agriculture, published by D. Appleton, is a textbook written for young farmers and schools in the 1850s, with questions for students printed at the foot of most pages. Chapters treat the formation and character of the soil, the character and varieties of manure, the mechanical character of the soil, and the nature of analysis.

An advertisement in the volume promises a larger sequel, The Earthworker, with fuller directions for manures and drainage. Practical rather than theoretical, the book teaches a farmer to test his ground, feed it wisely, and understand what his crops take from it. It remains a clear window on American farm science before the Civil War.
34650-a-gentleman-player-his-adventures-:
Robert Neilson Stephens wrote A Gentleman Player, a tale of secret work for Queen Elizabeth. L C Page and Company issued the novel in Boston in eighteen hundred ninety nine. Stephens had won sales with An Enemy to the King. A picture shows the queen with Harry Marryott at the front.

The tale opens at the first known show of Hamlet in March sixteen hundred one. A flag rose and a horn blew thrice in Southwark. Harry, an actor, draws the queen’s eye and her trust. Flight, a locked door, and a coach ride with a captive follow. Treason and love test his double role. He must play the gentleman and the player by turns.
39253-the-conspiracy-of-pontiac-and-the-:
Francis Parkman wrote a great history of the Indian war that followed the British conquest of Canada. The first of two volumes opens with a long survey of the native peoples. It treats their ranks of tribes, their modes of rule, and their social peace. The Iroquois stand at the center of that survey.

Parkman traces the league of the Iroquois, its myths, its eloquence, and its triumphs. He then passes to the Algonquin peoples and their changing fortunes. A second chapter, covering 1663 to 1763, sets France against England in America. It contrasts feudal Canada with the free towns of New England, and treats the Jesuit missions and the explorer La Salle. Parkman gave the volumes to Jared Sparks, the president of Harvard. The work is famed for its sweep and for the care of its telling.
40341-king-alfred-s-old-english-version-:
Henry Lee Hargrove turned King Alfred's Old English version of St Augustine's Soliloquies into modern English. Henry Holt published the volume at New York in 1904, as number twenty-two of the Yale Studies in English. Hargrove taught English at Baylor University. He dedicated the book to his brother Warren Penn Hargrove, who died on February 8, 1903, aged twenty-five. Alfred's own preface opens the text.

Alfred tells how he gathered staves, stud-shafts, and cross-beams in the wood. He took helves for his tools and timbers for his bows, the comeliest trees he could carry. In each tree he saw something he needed at home. He urges every able man with many wains to go to the same wood. There a man may load fair twigs, wind many a neat wall, and build a fair enclosure.
42957-modern-skepticism-a-course-of-lect:
Churchmen answer doubt in Modern Scepticism, a course of lectures delivered at the request of the Christian Evidence Society, printed in New York in 1871. Randolph made the book, by arrangement with the English publishers. An explanatory paper by Ellicott, lord bishop of Gloucester and Bristol, attends the lectures.

The preface commends the volume to the reader's serious consideration. The bishop's paper, though placed at the end, should be read early, it says: it gives the designs of the society and the plan of the lectures. The committee thanks the eminent men who lent able service to the great cause in hand. That cause is named plainly: the maintenance of the truth of the Christian Revelation. Design in Nature leads the course.
47521-life-and-times-of-her-majesty-caro:
Wraxall's Life and Times of Her Majesty Caroline Matilda, Queen of Denmark and Norway, appeared in London in 1864 in three volumes, of which this is the first. She was sister to George the Third of England. The queen's story, bound up with the fall of Struensee, was already famous as novel and opera material. Wraxall argues that new evidence changes the case.

His matter comes from the privy archives of Copenhagen, opened to him by the late king's leave, including the reports of the judges who passed the queen's divorce. He also draws on the memoirs of the Landgrave Charles of Hesse Cassel, on Reverdil, secretary to Christian the Seventh, and on his own grandfather's journals. The claim throughout is that the divorce rested on worthless evidence. Volume one builds that case from family documents and state papers.
49583-life-and-times-of-her-majesty-caro:
Life and Times of Her Majesty Caroline Matilda, volume two of three, by Sir C F Lascelles Wraxall, was printed in London in 1864. Caroline Matilda was queen of Denmark and Norway and sister of King George the Third of England. Wraxall drew on family documents and private state archives.

Chapter heads in this volume name a gathering storm, with an anonymous letter, incendiary placards, and sailors at Hirschholm. The second chapter is named The Sinking Ship, with Brandt letter of complaint and Struensee dignified answer. A mutiny of the guards fills the third chapter. Court intrigue, press freedom, and insulting pamphlets drive the fall of the queen and her minister Struensee. Readers should start at volume one for the rise that ends in ruin here.
55369-life-and-times-of-her-majesty-caro:
Volume three of Sir Lascelles Wraxall's Life and Times of Her Majesty Caroline Matilda was published in London in 1864 by Allen of Waterloo Place. Its subject is the queen of Denmark and Norway, sister of George the Third of England. Wraxall drew the work, as its title boasts, from family documents and private state archives. Three volumes make the set, and this one opens at the catastrophe.

The contents begin with the trial of Count Brandt: the indictment, his assault on the king, the alleged forgery, and the sentence proposed. The two counts follow, with Struensee's sentence and his despotism laid out, and then the execution itself, dated April 28. A high commission on the ten prisoners, and the fortress of Munkholm, come after.
doe-osti-3001274-laser-confocal-microsco:
Jonathan Gigax and Gabriel Longoria of Los Alamos pin down how much to trust a microscope in LA-UR-25-27800, issued 8 November 2025. The instrument is a Keyence VK-3050 laser confocal microscope, used to measure pit depths in corroded container coupons, the small metal samples that stand sentry for stored materials. A 20x objective does the work, stitching image arrays across 25-millimetre coupons in runs that can stretch to 48 hours per coupon.

Uncertainty hides in stage travel, scan duration and repeatability. Repeated scans of calibration samples, ten at a time at fixed locations with minimised travel, separated the error sources. Z-axis motion over long height ranges proved a real contributor, and equipment on-time another. The bottom line is practical: a combined depth uncertainty of plus or minus 0.25 micrometres captures the observed error across the study. Corrosion scientists can now quote pit depths with an honest error bar attached.
doe-osti-3002985-molecular-dynamics-simu:
Ian Winter, Eric Rothchild, and Michael Chandross simulate brazing at atomic scale in Sandia report SAND2025-14027, printed November 2025. The question is how well liquid silver, standing in for a silver braze alloy, wets zirconia ceramics whose oxygen content varies. Wetting decides whether a braze joint spreads and holds or beads up and fails.

Molecular dynamics runs computed the work of adhesion between the liquid metal and four solids: zirconium metal, two suboxides, and full zirconia. The phantom wall method estimated adhesion, and Young's equation converted it to a wetting angle. The silver surface tension came out at 0.67 joules per square meter. Results show a wetting transition as oxygen content falls: leaner oxides bond differently. Braze designers use such maps when joining ceramics to metals.
doe-osti-3376047-thermal-performance-of-:
Report INL/RPT-26-90669 from Idaho National Laboratory, by Kevin Tsai and Austin Fleming and dated February 2026, tests the heat control of a furnace built to qualify neutron sensors. The device gives sensors a known, steady heat while they sit in a neutron field. It was made for the AFRRI TRIGA reactor site. Its frame uses low-activation metals with small neutron cross sections, so the rig stays quiet in the beam. Three heat zones can be set to shape the heat along the tube.

Heat across the core zone held within six degrees Celsius. The rig reached a steady 350 degrees in about three hours. Its cooling time constant came out at three and a half hours. Outer faces stayed safe to touch, with the aluminum frame near room heat. The authors clear the device for sensor work and flag higher heat runs as a next step.
govdocs-archive_org-the-communist-party-: An FBI report in file HQ-116395, released under the Freedom of Information Act, examines the Communist Party USA and what the era called the Negro question. It records the party's stated position on Black Americans, as the bureau tracked it. The FBI watched the party for decades, and race was one of its constant concerns. The report shows both the party's line and the bureau's habits of watching it.
nasa-tm-19680018186-a-review-of-faciliti:
Seth B. Anderson and Laurel G. Schroers of Ames Research Center review low-speed flight test facilities and techniques in this paper. New classes of aircraft demand new and improved ways to test at low speed. Building novel aircraft is costly, so test methods must be trustworthy before full flight.

The authors survey the facilities available for low-speed work and the techniques used in them. They consider what new aircraft types require from those facilities. Gaps between current practice and future needs guide their review. The paper helps planners decide where to invest in test capability. It also helps engineers choose the right facility for a given low-speed program.
nasa-tm-19720019866-research-achievement:
Research Achievements Review, Volume 4, was issued May 30, 1972, as NASA TM X-64666. It covers quality and reliability assurance research at the Marshall Space Flight Center. The center's Science and Engineering Directorate published the review. Its theme, per the catalog record, is newer approaches to reliability engineering and quality control for aerospace work.

The contents open with two imaging studies. One develops solid-state radiographic X-ray image amplifiers, panels that make X-ray pictures without film. Tables and figures compare those panels with fluoroscopes and show images of a luggage interior and the inner fixture of a graphite-epoxy strut. A second study presents a neutron-radiation imaging system, with its own comparison tables. Together they show Marshall's quality researchers building better ways to inspect hardware without taking it apart.
podcast-dannyjones-xDTCN86kcQU:
Dead Sea Scrolls scholar Kipp Davis joins Danny Jones to say he lost his faith after he decoded the oldest Bible texts. Davis is a scholar of the scrolls and the Hebrew Bible. His tale is one of a faith undone by study.

Davis tells how years with the scrolls showed him cracks in the tales he was raised on. He walks through what the old texts truly say and where they clash with the church's tale. Jones asks what he holds to now. Listeners get a rare tale of a scholar whose work cost him his creed. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-0CrBPwS8OqU:
Welterweight fighter Daniel Rodriguez headlines Rogan's MMA Show number 180. Rodriguez built his record the hard way, through grit and volume. His style favors pressure and tough exchanges.

Rogan reviews his fights and what makes his game work. They talk about camps, cuts, and the grind below the spotlight. Rodriguez shares his path from hard years to the big stage. The episode suits fans who love working fighters more than stars: men who earn each shot and talk about the cost without complaint. Respect runs under every exchange in the room.
